briefing.text: PITFALL: A trajectory method always returns an ordering, even when the cells are really discrete clusters or when the 'dominant' axis is ambiguous; terminal groups can change purely with the choice of HVG number, n_pcs, n_neighbors and method, and orderings taken from UMAP/t-SNE coordinates are the most fragile. CHECK: on the same preprocessed data derive the axis three ways (PC1 of the HVGs, diffusion component 1, DPT/PAGA path) and confirm they agree (|Spearman| above about 0.8); repeat over a small grid (e.g. 1000/2000/4000 HVGs, 15/30/50 PCs, k=15/30) and measure the Jaccard overlap of terminal-group membership and of the top-N marker list; look at cell density along the axis to see whether it is a continuum or two/three separated clusters. IF FOUND: if the ends are discrete clusters, define the terminal groups as the Leiden clusters at the two extremes (ordered by mean axis value or PAGA path) rather than arbitrary pseudotime quantiles; if methods disagree, keep the axis that is stable across the grid; compute pseudotime in PCA/diffusion space, never on UMAP coordinates; report only markers that recur across settings.
briefing.reason: The whole answer hinges on which axis is called 'dominant' and how its two ends are cut; without a stability check the reported markers may reflect one arbitrary parameter choice.

briefing.text: PITFALL: The extremes of a diffusion component, DPT ordering or cluster-MST are easily captured by a handful of outlier cells or one tiny distant cluster (doublets, low-quality cells, a rare contaminant), and DPT additionally depends on an arbitrary root cell; the terminal groups then hold a few odd cells and their markers are unrepresentative. CHECK: inspect the distribution of DC1/PC1 (a long tail made by under about 2 percent of cells signals outliers); count the cells in each terminal group (each should be a substantial population, not a few dozen cells); rerun DPT rooted at each extreme and confirm the ordering is simply reversed; confirm in PAGA that the terminal clusters connect to the main body rather than sitting isolated. IF FOUND: set aside the outlier cluster if it is a contaminant/low-quality group and recompute, or use the next component; define each terminal group as a whole extreme cluster or a fixed tail (e.g. lowest and highest 10-20 percent of pseudotime), never single extreme cells. Direction/root does not matter for a two-ended marker contrast, so do not spend effort choosing a biological 'start'.
briefing.reason: It changes how terminal groups are defined and sized, and tells the team that root choice is not worth effort while outlier-driven ends are.

briefing.text: PITFALL: The file is a small pre-subset matrix (1689 cells x 20574 genes, raw integer UMI counts, mouse symbols, no obs/var annotation, no cell-type, cluster, sample or batch labels), so nothing guarantees every cell is a fibroblast. Non-fibroblast or fibroblast-adjacent cells (pericytes/vascular smooth muscle, mesothelial, endothelial, immune, epithelial/tumour cells, doublets) left in a 'CAF' matrix form a discrete outlier group that becomes one end of PC1/DC1, so the 'dominant trajectory' is really a cell-type contrast and the markers are lineage markers. CHECK: cluster coarsely and score canonical sets per cluster: fibroblast (Pdgfra, Col1a1, Col1a2, Dcn, Lum, Pdpn), mural (Rgs5, Mcam, Cspg4, Myh11, Des, Notch3), endothelial (Pecam1, Cdh5), immune (Ptprc), epithelial (Epcam, Krt8, Krt18), mesothelial (Msln, Upk3b, Wt1); look for clusters lacking fibroblast genes or weakly connected to the rest in the kNN/PAGA graph. IF FOUND: drop clearly non-mesenchymal clusters (immune, endothelial, epithelial, obvious doublets) and recompute the trajectory. Be careful with mural-like cells: several CAF studies deliberately keep Rgs5+/contractile cells as a CAF subtype, so do not strip mesenchymal cells by default; run the trajectory with and without them and report whether the terminal groups and top markers change.
briefing.reason: A contaminant cluster would silently become a terminal group; the team needs both the check and the warning not to over-filter mesenchymal cells in an unlabelled, already-subset file.

briefing.text: PITFALL: X holds raw counts, and the leading axis (PC1 or diffusion component 1) of scRNA-seq data often tracks technical quality (library size, genes detected, mitochondrial fraction, low-quality or dying cells) rather than biology; the terminal groups then become 'high-depth vs low-depth' cells and the markers are mito/ribosomal or simply abundant genes. CHECK: compute total counts, n_genes and percent mt- per cell; Spearman-correlate each with PC1-5, DC1 and the final pseudotime; compare these QC metrics between the two terminal groups. IF FOUND: filter low-quality outlier cells first, normalise properly (size factor + log1p; analytic Pearson residuals as a sensitivity check), and if a component is still mostly depth (|rho| above about 0.5-0.6 with no fibroblast-program signal) do not use it as the trajectory; take the next biological component. Do not blindly regress depth out, because cell size can genuinely differ between fibroblast states; instead confirm the axis survives the choice of normalisation.
briefing.reason: It can change which component is taken as the trajectory and warns against the reflex fix (regressing out depth) that could remove real biology.

briefing.text: PITFALL: Cell cycle is a strong confounder of trajectory inference; a proliferating cluster can become a terminal group and the top markers become cycle genes rather than CAF-state genes. In CAF data a 'cycling CAF' cluster has been described that is only the proliferating segment of another subtype, not a separate state. CHECK: score S and G2M gene sets (e.g. Mki67, Top2a, Cdk1, Ccnb1, Birc5, Pcna, Mcm2-7), correlate the scores with PC1-5, DC1 and pseudotime, and see whether either terminal group is enriched for cycling cells or cycle genes dominate the top marker list. IF FOUND: remove cell-cycle genes from the highly variable gene set (or regress the S/G2M scores) before PCA/neighbours, recompute the trajectory, and assign cycling cells to their parent state instead of treating them as an endpoint.
briefing.reason: If a cycling cluster ends up as a trajectory end, the reported markers would be proliferation genes; the check and fix alter preprocessing.

briefing.text: PITFALL: Enzymatic dissociation of solid tumours induces a stress / immediate-early program (Fos, Fosb, Jun, Junb, Egr1, Ier2, Ier3, Atf3, Dusp1, Zfp36, Klf4, Nr4a1, Hspa1a, Hspa1b) that is real transcription but a handling artefact; it has produced fake 'activated fibroblast' states and can be the major axis in stromal cells. CHECK: score this gene set per cell, correlate it with PC1/DC1/pseudotime, and count how many of the top markers between the terminal groups are immediate-early or heat-shock genes. IF FOUND: exclude these genes from the highly variable gene set (or regress the score) and recompute; if the axis disappears it was artefact. Do not remove genuine inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes in the same step; those are biology, only the IEG/heat-shock set is the artefact.
briefing.reason: A stress-driven axis would be mistaken for CAF heterogeneity; the item gives the specific gene set to test and the limit on what to remove.

briefing.text: PITFALL: Marker-ranking mechanics silently change the top-gene list. scanpy rank_genes_groups defaults to a t-test, ranks by test score, expects log-normalised data, compares each group against 'rest' unless a reference is given, lists only genes UP in the named group, and its logfoldchanges come from means of log1p values, so they are unreliable and explode for lowly expressed genes. Running it on scaled data or on an HVG-only subset drops or distorts true markers. CHECK: confirm the DE input is log1p-normalised counts for ALL genes (not .X after sc.pp.scale, not the HVG subset; keep a separate full-gene object and transfer only the group labels); confirm the contrast is terminal group A versus terminal group B directly (groups=[A], reference=B), not A versus all other cells including intermediates; use method='wilcoxon' with pts=True; recompute log2FC yourself from mean normalised counts with a pseudocount. IF FOUND: rerun as a direct two-group Wilcoxon contrast, require a minimum detection fraction in the higher group (about 25 percent or more) and a minimum fold change, rank by a robust effect size (Wilcoxon score/AUC, tie-break by logFC), and take top genes from BOTH directions (markers of end A and of end B) so the list distinguishes the two ends rather than describing only one.
briefing.reason: The deliverable is the top-marker list itself; default settings (vs-rest contrast, one direction only, HVG/scaled input) would produce a different list from a direct two-ended contrast.

briefing.text: PITFALL: Double dipping. The terminal groups are defined from the same expression data that is then tested, so p-values are inflated and essentially every gene that drove the axis is 'significant' even if the split is spurious; cells are also not independent replicates. Ranking or thresholding by p-value/adjusted p-value is therefore uninformative and favours highly expressed genes. CHECK: see whether thousands of genes pass FDR (a sign that p-values carry no ranking information); check that top genes have large effect sizes (AUC far from 0.5, clear difference in the fraction of cells expressing) rather than tiny shifts in abundant genes; as a robustness test, define the terminal groups on one random half of the genes or on thinned counts (count splitting) and test markers on the held-out part, or re-derive groups on bootstrap subsamples of cells. IF FOUND: rank markers by effect size (AUC / Cohen's d / logFC with a detection-fraction filter), not by p-value, and keep only genes that stay in the top list across the resampling or parameter grid.
briefing.reason: It changes the ranking criterion for the reported genes and supplies a concrete robustness test for the marker list.

briefing.text: PITFALL: Uninformative gene classes crowd the top-marker list. Mitochondrial (mt-), ribosomal (Rps/Rpl), Malat1 and unnamed clone/predicted genes (this file uses an older mouse annotation with names like RP23-..., RP24-..., Gm..., ...Rik) are among the most abundant features and rank highly on test score whenever the two ends differ in depth or quality; they are rarely what a 'marker gene' answer is judged on. CHECK: tabulate what fraction of the top 20-50 markers falls in these classes, and whether gene symbols need de-duplication (var_names_make_unique). IF FOUND: treat a list dominated by these classes as evidence that the axis is technical and fix it upstream (QC, normalisation, choice of component) rather than only hiding the genes; for the final list keep ranking on all genes but report named protein-coding genes with real effect sizes, and state the filter applied.
briefing.reason: It affects both the diagnosis of a technical axis and which genes are eligible for the reported list in this file's clone-name-heavy annotation.

briefing.text: PITFALL: Accepting a computed axis with no biological validation. As a sanity check only: published CAF scRNA-seq work most often describes the main CAF axis as running between an inflammatory / progenitor-like fibroblast state (literature examples for scoring: Il6, Cxcl12, Dpt; 'universal' Pi16+ fibroblasts) and a myofibroblastic / ECM-contractile state (literature examples for scoring: Acta2, Tagln, Myl9; matrix collagens), with antigen-presenting (MHC-II) and vascular/pericyte-like (Rgs5) groups as side populations. Mouse models differ, so this must NOT be used to choose the axis in advance or to fill in the answer. CHECK: after inferring the axis from the data, score the two literature programs per cell and see whether they change monotonically and in opposite directions along pseudotime, and whether the data-derived top markers are coherent secreted/ECM/contractile fibroblast genes rather than mito, ribosomal, cell-cycle, stress, haemoglobin or other-lineage genes. IF FOUND (no fibroblast-program gradient, or markers are artefact classes): suspect a confounder (contaminant cluster, cell cycle, depth, dissociation stress), fix it and recompute. If the data-derived axis is biologically coherent but differs from the literature expectation, trust the data and say so. The reported marker genes must come from the data contrast, never from these example genes.
briefing.reason: It gives the team an independent way to tell a biological axis from an artefact after the fact, with an explicit guard against hard-coding literature genes into the answer.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found a small Leiden cluster (a few dozen cells) whose top markers are epithelial keratins (Krt8, Krt18, Epcam and similar), with a lower fibroblast score and high UMI depth, and it removed that cluster before computing the trajectory. Your contaminant check reported these markers as low and you kept all cells. Check whether your check was an average over all cells or over coarse clusters, which would hide a group of that size: look at these markers per cluster at a finer Leiden resolution and per cell. If such a group exists in your data, where does it sit on your axis, is any of it inside your terminal groups, and do the axis, the terminal cells or your top list change when it is left out? Does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team defined the terminal groups as the whole Leiden clusters at the two extremes of the axis rather than as fixed-fraction tails, and it repeated the analysis over a grid of HVG numbers, PC numbers and neighbour numbers. It saw that the axis itself is stable across the grid but that which cells fall in the end groups, and part of the top marker list, are not. Your robustness check varied only the tail fraction on one preprocessing setting. Check how much of your top list survives when you vary the number of HVGs, PCs and neighbours, and when the terminal groups are the extreme clusters instead of the tails. Also look at the cell density along your axis: is it a continuum or separated groups, and what does that say about how an end should be defined? Does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: your notes do not record the mechanics of the marker test, and the other team found that these mechanics change the top-gene list. Record which gene universe the test ran on (all genes or only the HVGs), which matrix (log-normalised or scaled), and whether it was a direct contrast of one end against the other or each end against the rest. The other team also saw a cycling cluster in the data and unnamed-clone gene symbols (Gm, Rik, RP-type) plus ribosomal genes in the annotation; it kept cell-cycle and immediate-early genes out of the HVGs and screened the reported genes for detection rate, effect size and gene class. Check whether your high-count cluster 2 is that cycling group, whether cell-cycle genes among your HVGs move the axis or the terminal cells, and whether any gene in your reported list is detected in few cells, has a small fold change, or belongs to one of those classes. Does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team defined the terminal groups as fixed-fraction tails of the first diffusion component and found its top list unchanged across three tail fractions. Your terminal groups are whole Leiden clusters, each a much larger share of the cells than such a tail, and your own grid showed that the membership of the end clusters shifts strongly with settings while the axis does not. Check what fraction of each of your terminal clusters lies in the extreme tail of the axis and how far each cluster reaches toward the middle, and compare the top list from your clusters with the top list from tails on your own data. You recorded that a tail definition changed a sizeable part of your list: which genes change, and which definition matches 'the two ends of the dominant trajectory' in the task text? Does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team reported its genes in strict rank order from a single two-group contrast, with no detection filter, no fold-change filter, no gene-class exclusion and no preference for genes that recur across settings. Your reported list was chosen to favour recurrence across your grid, after those filters, so it is not the plain ranking of any one run. Write down the strict top-ranked genes of your primary run with no filter and no recurrence preference, and list which genes each step (detection filter, fold-change filter, gene-class exclusion, recurrence preference) adds or removes. Which of those steps does the task text ask for, and which genes in your final list depend on a step it does not ask for? Does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team kept every cell in the file and used the plain top HVGs, with nothing excluded from them; its contaminant check found epithelial, immune and endothelial markers low, and it treated the file as CAFs throughout, as the task text does. You removed a small keratin-positive cluster and kept cell-cycle, immediate-early, ribosomal and unnamed-clone genes out of the HVGs. Check, on your data, what each of these two choices does on its own: with the cluster left in and with a plain HVG set, do the axis, the terminal groups and the top list change, and where did the removed cells sit on the axis? Check also what evidence separates a contaminant or doublet from a keratin-expressing fibroblast-lineage population in that cluster (fibroblast and collagen genes per cell, doublet-like depth, co-expression). Does that change your method?

referee.difference: Both use DC1 (diffusion map, ~PC1) 15% tails as terminal groups and a Wilcoxon contrast; they share 15/20 genes. They differ in (a) ranking rule: X interleaves top-10 up from each end (balanced), Y ranks all genes by |AUC-0.5| strictly (13 iCAF-end, 7 myCAF-end); (b) Y drops a 25-cell Epcam+ cluster and filters HVGs. Disputed: X-only Tagln, Col5a2, Sfrp4, Acta2, Thbs2; Y-only Tnxb, Htra3, Efemp1, Serpina3n, Igfbp7.
referee.test: code/test.py: neutral rerun (log-norm, 2000 HVG, PCA20, kNN15, diffmap, DC1 15% tails, no cell removal), scanpy Wilcoxon hi vs lo on all genes; rank every disputed gene by |z|; build both a strict |z| top-20 and a balanced 10+10 list.
referee.expected_if_x: X's unique genes rank in the strict top 20 and Y's unique genes fall outside, or the strict list is itself balanced, so the ranking rule makes no difference.
referee.expected_if_y: Y's unique genes rank in the strict top 20 and X's unique genes rank lower, under neutral preprocessing as well as Y's.
referee.outcome: The axis reproduced (DC1 vs PC1 r=-0.975). Wilcoxon |z| is saturated: all 25 genes have |z| between 17.1 and 19.5 (AUC near 1), so their order is decided by small differences. Strict top 20 holds 16 X genes and 17 Y genes. Y-only Htra3(15), Serpina3n(16) and Tnxb(18) rank in, but so do X-only Sfrp4(12) and Col5a2(20). Efemp1 ranks 22, Igfbp7 34, Tagln 27, Thbs2 36, Acta2 37. The balanced 10+10 list matches X at 17/20. Each list reproduces under its own ranking rule, and the data does not decide which rule is right.
referee.reason: The split comes from a ranking convention (balanced per-end vs global strict) that the task text does not specify, and the disputed genes are all near-perfect separators with saturated, nearly tied statistics. Under neutral preprocessing each candidate has weak genes: X has Acta2/Thbs2/Tagln (ranks 27-37), Y has Igfbp7/Efemp1 (22-34).

questions.question: In scanpy's rank_genes_groups with method='wilcoxon' and an explicit reference group (a direct two-group contrast), is the ordering of genes by the returned score the same as ordering by AUC (U statistic divided by the product of group sizes), with and without tie correction? Does the function list only genes that are up in the tested group, which gene universe and matrix does it use by default (use_raw, layers), and how many genes does it return by default?
questions.why: One team ranked by AUC and the other by Wilcoxon score. If these orderings are identical for fixed groups, the statistic cannot explain the disagreement and the teams can concentrate on group definition and filtering. The defaults matter because one team did not record its gene universe or matrix.

questions.question: In established trajectory-inference tools and tutorials (diffusion pseudotime, PAGA, Slingshot, Palantir, CellRank), how are the 'terminal' cell groups at the two ends of a single dominant trajectory defined by default or by convention: as the clusters at the ends of the ordering, as a fixed quantile of pseudotime, or as individual tip cells? Is there published guidance on how large an end group should be when it is used for a two-group differential-expression contrast?
questions.why: The main difference between the teams is whether an end is a whole cluster or a fixed-fraction tail of the axis. A documented convention would let both teams judge their definition against something other than their own preference.

questions.question: In single-cell RNA-seq of cancer-associated fibroblasts, has a small keratin-expressing population (Krt8, Krt18, mesothelial-type markers) been described as a genuine fibroblast-lineage or mesothelial-derived CAF subtype rather than epithelial contamination or doublets? What criteria do published analyses use to tell these apart, and do they usually keep or remove such cells before trajectory analysis of CAF states?
questions.why: One team removed a small keratin-positive, high-depth cluster as a contaminant and the other kept all cells. Whether such cells can legitimately belong to the CAF compartment decides which rows should be kept before the axis and markers are computed.

findings.question: In scanpy's rank_genes_groups with method='wilcoxon' and an explicit reference group, is ordering by score the same as ordering by AUC, with and without tie correction? Does it list only up genes; which gene universe/matrix (use_raw, layers) and how many genes by default?
findings.answer: Without tie correction (the default, tie_correct=False), yes. For fixed groups the score is the Mann-Whitney z=(U-n1*n2/2)/sqrt(n1*n2*(n1+n2+1)/12), a strictly increasing function of U and therefore of AUC=U/(n1*n2), so both give the same gene order. With tie_correct=True each gene's denominator is scaled by its own tie factor, so the order can differ from AUC, mainly for sparse genes with many zeros. The formula is the standard normal approximation: the fetched source file was truncated before the scoring code, and the docs only say the score is the z-score behind the p-value. Defaults: use_raw=None (uses adata.raw if present, else .X), layer=None, mask_var=None (all genes in the matrix used), n_genes=None (all genes returned), rankby_abs=False. Genes are sorted by descending signed score, so genes up in the tested group come first and genes up in the reference come last with negative scores. Not only up genes are returned, but the top-N of one call describes only the tested group. The statistic cannot explain the teams' disagreement; group definition, gene universe (raw/all genes vs HVG-subset .X) and filtering can.

findings.question: How are terminal cell groups at the two ends of a single dominant trajectory defined by default/convention in DPT, PAGA, Slingshot, Palantir, CellRank; is there guidance on end-group size for a two-group DE contrast?
findings.answer: No tool I read defines ends as a fixed pseudotime quantile. Slingshot: lineages are MST paths from a start cluster to leaf clusters, and end.clus forces chosen clusters to be leaves, so ends are whole clusters. scanpy DPT: needs one root cell (uns['iroot']); its docs recommend dpt for pseudotime only and PAGA (nodes are clusters) for branch structure. Palantir: identify_terminal_states returns individual terminal cells, and run_palantir takes terminal states as single cell names. CellRank GPCCA: terminal states are macrostates (soft cluster groups) restricted to a set number of the most likely cells. I recall the default as n_cells=30 but did not see it on the pages read. I found no published guidance on how large an end group should be for a DE contrast. The cluster-at-each-end convention (Slingshot/PAGA) is the best documented; a quantile tail is an analyst's choice.

findings.question: Has a small keratin-expressing (Krt8, Krt18, mesothelial-marker) population been described as a genuine fibroblast-lineage or mesothelial-derived CAF subtype rather than contamination/doublets; what criteria distinguish them; are they kept or removed before CAF trajectory analysis?
findings.answer: Yes. Mesothelial-derived antigen-presenting CAFs are established. Elyada et al. 2019 defined MHC-II/Cd74+ apCAFs after depleting CD45/CD31/EpCAM cells. Huang et al. 2022 (Cancer Cell) used lineage tracing to show mouse PDAC apCAFs come from mesothelial cells; their clusters express Msln, Upk3b, Krt19, Ezr, Nkain4 and Lrrn4 plus MHC-II genes and gain fibroblast features. A 2025 pan-cancer atlas finds mesothelial-like apCAFs in most tumour types. Criteria for a genuine CAF: Epcam negative, co-expression of fibroblast genes (Pdpn/Col1a1/Dcn), the mesothelial gene set and MHC-II, and no tumour/epithelial program. A liver CAF review states (seen only in a search snippet, full text not read) that Krt8/Krt19-co-expressing CAF clusters can be epithelial/CAF doublets. High depth plus keratins is a doublet warning sign, to be checked with a doublet score. The pages read do not set a convention for keeping or removing such cells before trajectory analysis. Keep them if they are Epcam-negative and mesothelial/MHC-II-positive, remove them if they are Epcam-positive or doublet-like, and report results both ways.
